summary: Describes common problems seen in RADIUS implementations and suggests fixes. Where earlier RADIUS specifications were ambiguous or wrong, it clarifies them. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RADIUS is the protocol a network device uses to ask a central server whether a user may get access. This RFC lists the problems that turned up when different makers built RADIUS servers and clients, and settles each one with a clear rule.

subtitle: Common RADIUS implementation problems and the fixes the IETF settled on.

tldr.problem: RADIUS has been deployed for years and its specifications contain ambiguities, errors and gaps, so implementations of the same protocol do not always behave the same way.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC walks through the problems seen in practice, from the State attribute to retransmission timers, duplicate detection, accounting attributes and the meaning of Access-Reject, and states what each side should do instead.
tldr.outcome: The document clarifies and updates four earlier RADIUS specifications and gives implementers concrete rules that make different RADIUS deployments behave more alike.

facts.label: Duplicate cache entry lifetime
facts.value: No less than 5 and no more than 30 seconds

today: RFC 5080 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2007. It updates RFC 2865, RFC 2866, RFC 2869 and RFC 3579, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why RADIUS Implementations Disagree
sections.content:
RADIUS clients and servers are deployed in growing numbers, and the original specifications leave room for different readings. This document describes the issues that show up in practice and suggests fixes, clarifying ambiguities and errors in the earlier RADIUS specifications where that applies.

The terms used throughout come from the protocol itself. A Network Access Server (NAS) is the device that gives a user access to the network; it is also the authenticator in IEEE 802.1X terms, or the RADIUS client. A service is what the NAS offers the user, such as network access over 802.11 or over PPP. Each service the NAS provides is a session, which starts when service is first provided and ends when service stops, and each session generates its own start and stop accounting record. To silently discard a packet means to drop it without further processing, though the implementation SHOULD be able to log the error and record the event in a statistics counter.
sections.plainLanguage: Different teams built RADIUS servers and clients from the same written specification, and the specification was loose in places. This RFC gathers the disagreements that came out of that and gives one answer for each.

sections.title: The State Attribute and Multi-Round Logins
sections.content:
The State attribute ties several Access-Request and Access-Challenge packets into one authentication session. The server sends it in an Access-Challenge, and the client MUST send it back unmodified in the Access-Request that answers the challenge.

Some clients did not use State to tell a restarted Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) exchange apart from the continuation of an ongoing one. The RFC therefore says that Access-Requests which are part of an ongoing Access-Request and Access-Challenge process SHOULD contain a State attribute, and that servers implementing authentication mechanisms that need several rounds SHOULD include one in their Access-Challenge packets.

The rules on when State must, must not and should not appear are precise. Only values that the client received from a server in an Access-Accept, Access-Challenge, CoA-Request or Disconnect-Request may be used. An Access-Request that starts a new or restarted authentication run MUST NOT contain State, even if the same user and port received one earlier. An Access-Request with a Service-Type of Authorize Only (17) MUST contain State, one with a Service-Type of Call Check (10) SHOULD NOT contain it, and any other Access-Request that performs authorization checks MUST contain State.

Call Check is the case of pre-screening on the endpoint identifier alone, such as a phone number or a Media Access Control (MAC) address. The NAS has no way to obtain a suitable State value there, and reusing the User-Name and User-Password with the same value, such as a MAC address, is NOT RECOMMENDED, because it hands an attacker both the clear text and the cipher text of the password field.

Any Access-Request that performs authorization checks SHOULD carry a Message-Authenticator attribute. A response to such a request MUST NOT contain confidential information about any user unless the request carried a State attribute, in which case the server MAY return confidential information about that user and MUST NOT return it about any other user. An authorization check without a State attribute MUST be answered with an Access-Reject.
sections.plainLanguage: The State attribute is a label the server hands out and the client returns unchanged. It tells the server that a series of messages belong to one login attempt, so the server can tell a new attempt from a continuation.

sections.title: Retransmission Timers and Congestion Backoff
sections.content:
RADIUS clients retransmit requests, and some implementations do it far too eagerly, with timeouts of one second or less and no congestion backoff. At scale this leads to congestion collapse. The RFC's example is a network with 3,000 NAS devices that all use a fixed one second timer: after a power failure they generate 3,000 RADIUS Access-Requests per second, which is enough to overwhelm most RADIUS servers.

The suggested fixes are jitter, so that clients do not all retry at the same moment, and congestive backoff, which the RFC says implementations SHOULD support even though a complex algorithm is not required. The timers follow the model used by the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6, and the same variables are borrowed from it.

Five variables describe the behavior. RT is the retransmission timeout. IRT is the initial retransmission time, with a default of 2 seconds. MRC is the maximum retransmission count, a default of 5 attempts. MRT is the maximum retransmission time, a default of 16 seconds. MRD is the maximum retransmission duration, a default of 30 seconds. RAND is the randomization factor, a random number with a uniform distribution between -0.1 and +0.1. The random number does not have to be cryptographically sound, but the algorithm SHOULD produce a different sequence each time it runs.

The first transmission uses RT = IRT + RAND*IRT. Each later retransmission uses RT = 2*RTprev + RAND*RTprev. If RT exceeds MRT, it becomes MRT + RAND*MRT. A value of zero for MRT means there is no upper limit. MRD MUST be set and SHOULD be between 5 and 30 seconds. The exchange fails when the sender has transmitted the message MRC times or when MRD seconds have passed, whichever comes first. For Accounting-Request packets the defaults for MRC, MRD and MRT SHOULD be zero, so that accounting information is not discarded before it is recorded.
sections.plainLanguage: A client that gets no answer retries, and the wait between retries grows each time. A small random amount is added to each wait so that thousands of clients do not all retry at the same instant.

sections.title: Duplicate Detection and Cached Responses
sections.content:
RADIUS runs over the User Datagram Protocol (UDP), so a retransmitted request can arrive twice, and packets can arrive in a different order from the one in which they were sent. The server can recognize a duplicate by the client source IP address, source UDP port and Identifier within a short span of time.

Servers MUST implement duplicate detection for Access-Request packets, and MUST also cache the responses they send, whether Access-Accept, Access-Challenge or Access-Reject. A valid duplicate for which a response has already been sent MUST be answered by resending the original response without reprocessing the request. A duplicate for which no response has yet been sent MUST be silently discarded. Without this, a server can process one authentication twice and conclude that a user logged in twice.

Cache entries SHOULD be purged after a time that is no less than 5 seconds and no more than 30 seconds, because after about 30 seconds most clients and users have given up. Entries MUST also be purged when a valid Access-Request matches a cached one in source address, source port, Identifier and receiving socket but carries a different Request Authenticator. A request that contains a Message-Authenticator attribute is processed as described in RFC 3580, and packets with an invalid Message-Authenticator MUST NOT affect the cache. Requests without a Message-Authenticator always affect the cache even though they can be forged trivially, so servers may be configured to require that attribute and to discard requests that lack it. Clients SHOULD include a Message-Authenticator in every Access-Request.

On the client side, Identifiers MUST NOT be reused for a source IP address and source UDP port until a valid response arrives or the request times out, and clients SHOULD allocate them by a least recently used method. Clients do not have to detect duplicates: they process the first response with a valid Response Authenticator and silently discard any later response, exactly as they would an unsolicited one.
sections.plainLanguage: If a server gets the same request twice, it must not run the authentication twice. It remembers the answer it already gave and sends that answer again, so the user is not counted as having logged in twice.

sections.title: Accounting Attributes and Their Types
sections.content:
Several accounting points are clarifications of earlier text. RFC 2866 says that the octet, packet, session time and terminate cause attributes can only appear in an Accounting-Request whose Acct-Status-Type is Stop, while RFC 2869 envisages an Interim-Update record carrying all of them except the terminate cause. The RFC resolves the conflict in favour of RFC 2869: those attributes are allowed in an interim accounting record.

Two attributes are described with the wrong type. RFC 2866 gives Acct-Session-Id as a String but then says it should be a string of UTF-8 encoded characters; the RFC calls this a typographical error and says Acct-Session-Id is of type Text. The Acct-Multi-Session-Id attribute is also defined as a String, and its summary line mistakenly refers to Acct-Session-Id. The RFC says this attribute SHOULD be treated as Text.

For the Request Authenticator of an Accounting-Request, the RFC adds text that the earlier specification lacked. The field MUST contain the correct data, invalid packets are silently discarded, and although some early implementations always set the field to all zeros, new clients MUST use the correct algorithm and new servers MUST silently discard invalid packets.

A locally configured Interim-Accounting-Interval on the NAS is described too strongly elsewhere. A NAS may hold a minimum value based on its own resources, and that value should not be overridden by a smaller one from an Access-Accept, though a larger one may override it. The intent is that accounting updates arrive often enough to limit lost billing but seldom enough to avoid overloading the network.

The counter formulas in the RADIUS Management Information Base (MIB) have inconsistencies. The variable named Successfully Received can come out negative, and the equation that adds AccessRequests, PendingRequests and ClientTimeouts should end in Successfully Transmitted rather than Successfully Received. The RFC explains the issues without changing the object definitions, and notes that retransmissions should be treated consistently when counting pending requests.
sections.plainLanguage: Some accounting attributes were described with the wrong type or with contradictory rules about when they may appear. The RFC says which reading is correct and adds the missing rules for invalid accounting packets.

sections.title: What an Access-Reject Must Mean
sections.content:
An Access-Reject denies access to the requested service. It cannot be used to provision services: the only attributes it may carry are those needed to route the message, such as Proxy-State, those that tell the user access was denied, such as an EAP-Message holding an EAP-Failure, and those that carry an error message, such as Reply-Message or Error-Cause. If limited access is wanted, the server sends an Access-Accept with attributes that provision it.

The RFC finds that this rule has been misunderstood. RFC 2869 describes an Access-Reject carrying a Password-Retry attribute in the middle of a continuing authentication conversation, where an Access-Challenge is what the semantics call for. The RFC makes three recommendations: new specifications and implementations MUST NOT use Access-Reject where Access-Challenge semantics are intended; Access-Reject MUST mean denial of access, and the NAS MUST NOT send any further Access-Request for that user session; and new deployments of the ARAP extension SHOULD use Access-Challenge in the conversations RFC 2869 describes. It also corrects the attribute table of RFC 2869, moving Password-Retry (attribute 75) from the Reject column to the Challenge column, and notes that its use in EAP authentication is deprecated and that it can be used only for ARAP authentication.

RADIUS is also used well beyond network access, as a back end for Voice over IP, HTTP, FTP and machine logins. In those cases an Access-Reject MUST be read as a rejection of the request for service, and the client MUST NOT offer that service to the user. Where a user asks for several services that are independent, the deployment MUST treat the RADIUS sessions as independent, so a rejected multi-link connection does not tear down earlier ones, and a rejected Voice over IP attempt does not end a dialup session.
sections.plainLanguage: An Access-Reject is a plain refusal and nothing else. It must not be used to continue a conversation, because the server has no way to say what the client should do next. A refusal ends that request.

sections.title: Addressing and Other Loose Ends
sections.content:
Link-local addresses are unique only on the local link, so a NAS SHOULD NOT use one in a NAS-IPv6-Address or NAS-IP-Address attribute, and a server SHOULD NOT count such an attribute towards the requirement that one of those attributes or a NAS-Identifier be present. A NAS with more than one global address, which a dual stack host or a host on several VLANs will have, is RECOMMENDED to include the NAS-Identifier attribute, because the address attributes allow only one value. The server MUST use the source IP address of the RADIUS UDP packet to decide which shared secret to use, so a client that sends from more than one source address needs a shared secret for each of them.

Other points are settled briefly. The Idle-Timeout attribute sets the maximum number of consecutive seconds of idle connection allowed before the session ends or the user is prompted, and idle is defined by local policy in the absence of other attributes, since the NAS may count only the traffic its filters include. For an EAP-Response/Identity with a zero length Type-Data field, the NAS is RECOMMENDED either to omit the User-Name attribute or to put the Calling-Station-Id in it and send a Calling-Station-Id attribute as well; such an identity is not a request for privacy, since RFC 4282 does not allow a zero length Network Access Identifier.

When a response arrives after retransmissions, the contents of an Access-Request SHOULD NOT change between transmissions. If they must change, for example to add an Event-Timestamp attribute, responses to earlier transmissions MUST be silently discarded and the response to the current request is the definitive one. The RFC notes that a fixed retransmission timeout of 30 seconds is common and repeats the earlier advice to use congestive backoff.

Finally, the Framed-IPv6-Prefix attribute carries a prefix and route to configure for the user. The allowed prefix length of up to 128 bits is too broad, because it is unclear what a NAS should do with a prefix more granular than a /64. The RFC concludes that the attribute is meant for the link between the NAS and customer premises equipment when a /64 or larger prefix is assigned, and that a prefix the customer equipment delegates for its own use belongs in the Delegated-IPv6-Prefix attribute instead.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the smaller questions that had no single agreed answer: which address identifies the server, how long a client waits for an answer, what to do when the user name is empty, and how a prefix for the customer link should be treated.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The contents of the State attribute are visible both to the RADIUS client and to anyone watching the protocol, so server implementations should make sure that State does not disclose sensitive information.

The duplicate detection cache described in Section 2.2.2 is vulnerable when Access-Request packets do not carry a Message-Authenticator attribute. If the server accepts requests without one, RADIUS packets can be forged trivially, and cache entries can be forcibly expired, which removes the value of the cache. The RFC points to the mitigations in RFC 3579, or to requiring the presence of a Message-Authenticator as described in Sections 2.1.1 and 2.2.2.

Since RADIUS is used for authentication, authorization and accounting in many kinds of network and application, deployments are exposed to all of the threats that apply to other RADIUS applications. The RFC refers to RFC 2865, RFC 2607, RFC 3162, RFC 3579 and RFC 3580 for that discussion.
sections.plainLanguage: The State value travels in the clear, so it must not carry anything secret. The duplicate cache is also weaker than it looks unless every request is signed with a Message-Authenticator.
